title: Why Siblings Differ
text:
Parents of several children often marvel at how different their children are, despite the same house, the same parents and the same rules. In 1987, the behavioral geneticists Robert Plomin and Denise Daniels published a landmark review that took this puzzle seriously.

They gathered results from studies of twins, adopted children and ordinary families. One striking finding was that adopted children who grew up together in the same home, but shared no genes, ended up barely more similar in personality than strangers. Biological siblings were more alike, but mostly to the extent expected from the genes they share.

The implication was surprising. The parts of the environment that siblings share, such as family income, parents' education or the general atmosphere of the home, seemed to do little to make siblings alike in personality and many other traits. What mattered more was the nonshared environment: the experiences that differ for each child in the same family. These include being treated differently by parents, being older or younger, having different friends, teachers and illnesses, and chance events.

Plomin and Daniels argued that the important question was not how families differ from one another, but how each child in a family experiences a different family.
lesson: Each of your children lives in a different family, even under one roof. Pay attention to the distinct experience each child is having.
source: Plomin, R., and Daniels, D. (1987). Why are children in the same family so different from one another? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 10(1), 1-16.
caveat: Later research has found it hard to identify specific nonshared experiences that explain much of the difference, and shared family environment matters more for some outcomes such as education.
